concept_options.title: The Countdown
concept_options.hook: Dive in. Red vanishes at 5m. Orange at 25. Yellow at 50. Only blue survives. Here's why.
concept_options.visual_approach: Animated depth gauge counter descending through milestones. Stat cards appear at each color-loss event (5m, 25m, 50m, 200m). Word-level karaoke captions throughout. Remotion text_card and stat_card scene components.
concept_options.tone: Calm, curious, wonder-driven. Submarine documentary feel.
concept_options.target_audience: General adults curious about ocean science
key_points: Red light is absorbed within 5 meters of the ocean surface
Orange disappears by 25m, yellow by 50m — only blue penetrates to 200m
Water molecules absorb longer wavelengths via O-H bond resonance
95% of the ocean has zero sunlight — the deep is black, not blue
concept_options.core_message: The ocean is blue because water molecules eat red light — color by color, meter by meter.
concept_options.cta: Next time you look at the ocean, picture every color being stripped away beneath the surface.
grounded_in: NOAA depth-specific color disappearance data: red 5m, orange 25m, yellow 50m, blue only at 200m
Pope & Fry 1997: 50x absorption ratio red vs blue
Audience common question: why do underwater photos look green/grey?
concept_options.why_this_works: The descent structure creates a visceral countdown audiences can feel. Each depth milestone is a satisfying beat. The underserved gap in existing content is the precise depth-by-depth data; this concept delivers it in the most intuitive format possible — you are descending. Grounded in NOAA data and a high-surprise audience pain point: holiday underwater photos looking washed out.

concept_options.title: The Myth Bust
concept_options.hook: The ocean would still be blue under a completely grey sky. Its blue is not borrowed from above.
concept_options.visual_approach: Open on sky-reflection misconception card. Shatter transition reveals the truth. Molecular diagram (Mermaid SVG) shows O-H bond absorbing red photons. Closes on scale stat card: 95% of the ocean has no light at all.
concept_options.tone: Calm curiosity with gentle 'wait, actually' energy.
concept_options.target_audience: Adults who know the 'reflects the sky' answer and want the real explanation
key_points: The sky-reflection explanation is incomplete — deep water is blue even under a grey sky
Water's O-H bond absorbs red light; blue is what remains after absorption
The ocean's color is intrinsic to water molecules, not borrowed from above
concept_options.core_message: The ocean's blue is not borrowed from the sky — it lives in the water molecules themselves.
concept_options.cta: Share this with someone who gave you the sky-reflection answer.
grounded_in: Audience misconception: 'it reflects the sky' — dominant but incomplete explanation online
Mobley 2006: intrinsic absorption spectrum of water
concept_options.why_this_works: Myth-busting format creates an immediate 'wait, really?' engagement hook. The sky-reflection misconception is the dominant online explanation, making the correction genuinely surprising to most viewers. The counterintuitive claim in the hook drives shares and retention.

concept_options.title: The 50x Molecule
concept_options.hook: Water absorbs red light 50 times faster than blue. That one number explains everything.
concept_options.visual_approach: Lead with bar-chart stat card showing wavelength absorption spectrum. 50x ratio headline card. Transition to O-H bond vibrational resonance explanation via Mermaid diagram. Close with ocean depth scale.
concept_options.tone: Sciency, satisfying, mechanism-first. For viewers who want the quantitative physics.
concept_options.target_audience: Adults who want the mechanism, not just the phenomenon
key_points: Red absorption coefficient 0.65 m⁻¹ vs blue 0.013 m⁻¹ — a 50x difference (Pope & Fry 1997)
O-H bond vibrational resonance explains why water absorbs red photons specifically
This molecular selectivity, not sky reflection, determines ocean color
concept_options.core_message: One number — 50x — is the whole story of ocean color.
concept_options.cta: Now you know why underwater photography needs a red filter below 10 meters.
grounded_in: Pope & Fry 1997: absorption coefficients 0.65 m⁻¹ (red 700nm) vs 0.013 m⁻¹ (blue 450nm)
Mobley 2006: O-H bond vibrational resonance absorption mechanism
B&H Photo underwater photography: red filters used below ~10m
concept_options.why_this_works: The 50x ratio anchors the physics in one memorable, striking number. Mechanism-first structure serves the underserved gap of viewers who found 'sky reflection' answers unsatisfying. The data-narrative format is fresh against the mostly qualitative existing content on this topic.

selected_concept.rationale: User selected Option A — The Countdown. Depth-descent journey with milestone stat cards is the most visceral and intuitive structure for this content.

stages.approach: Write 60-second narration script (~150 words at 2.5 words/second). Countdown structure: hook at surface, red gone at 5m, orange at 25m, yellow at 50m, mechanism reveal (O-H bond in plain language), closing scale punch (95% of ocean has no light). Word-level timing markers included.

Map script segments to Remotion scene components: text_card for hook and narration beats, stat_card for depth milestones (5m/25m/50m/200m), callout for the 50x absorption ratio. Define frame timing, transition types, depth-gauge animated visual layer.

voice_selection.rationale: Only available TTS provider under zero-key constraint. Piper local TTS is free, offline, and produces natural-sounding English narration suitable for a documentary tone.
voice_selection.delivery_style: Warm expert narrator. Calm, curious, measured pace. Documentary feel — not corporate.
voice_selection.pacing_policy: Natural conversational pace with 0.5-second pauses at each depth milestone for visual emphasis. Slight slowdown on the final scale reveal.

music_source.mood_direction: Ambient underwater or calm instrumental. 60BPM or slower. Minimal melodic line. Blue, deep, expansive feel. No drums or upbeat elements.
